reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .365 xwOBA sits at the 91st percentile, which is elite company, but the strikeout rate tells a different story: 26.7% K%, bottom fifth of the league. That gap between his contact quality and his contact frequency is the whole tension in this profile, and the reason his xBA lands at just .256 while his xSLG pushes .472. The strikeout rate is the dependency; everything else is already there.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The .419 xwOBA and 20.8% barrel rate are both 100th-percentile figures, and they're built on a 95.1 mph average exit velocity that makes the raw power look earned rather than accidental. The catch is a 28.6% strikeout rate that lives in the 12th percentile, a real drag on contact value even with a 16.8% walk rate keeping the OBP healthy and an .387 projected OBP showing how much the walks actually rescue the line. If the swing-and-miss stays where it is, you're looking at a .263 hitter who slugs .524 with 37 home runs, a classic power-over-contact profile that still plays at full-season scale because the discipline is genuine. The whole thing hinges on whether he can trim even a few points off that whiff rate as pitchers accumulate a book on him — if he does, this becomes a true middle-of-the-order bat; if he doesn't, he's still very useful, just a little more volatile than the raw Statcast numbers make him look.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The Statcast batting profile sits at 98th percentile across xwOBA, xBA, and xSLG simultaneously, and the pitching xERA of 2.71 is just as legitimate. What makes this profile unusual isn't any single number: it's that the contact quality on both sides of the ball belongs to different tiers of the sport, and he's doing both at once. The one genuine tension in the hitting profile is the 30.3% whiff rate against a 14.0% walk rate; he chases at a middling clip and swings through enough pitches that a disciplined game-plan can carve into the counting stats, which is where the projection's .289/.395/.553 line absorbs some friction relative to the raw Statcast ceiling. On the mound, a 98.1 mph fastball pairing with 2488 rpm spin rate and a 30.4% whiff rate explains the contact suppression, opponents averaging 87.4 mph exit velocity against him, and the only structural concern is a 7.6% walk rate that limits how deep into games the profile holds.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact rates are the only thing standing between De La Cruz and a legitimate star profile. A 93.9 mph average exit velocity sits in the 98th percentile, and a 14.4% barrel rate paired with 51.7% hard contact isn't a guy running hot on a short sample, it's a genuine elite batted-ball profile, which is why the .368 xwOBA tracks cleanly to the projected .846 OPS. The problem is a 28.2% whiff rate that lands in the 30th percentile, creating real drag on what the raw power and speed deserve, and if pitchers continue to exploit the swing-and-miss, the 26.7% strikeout rate will pull that batting average back toward the projection floor. If the contact catches up, even partly, to what the quality-of-contact numbers suggest it should, a 28-homer, 32-steal shortstop posting an .846 OPS at 24 is an MVP-conversation player; if it doesn't, you're still looking at a high-impact, two-category contributor who's leaving a lot of talent in the dirt.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The 14.1% barrel rate is doing a lot of work here, and the Statcast profile explains why: an .471 xSLG that nearly matches his projected .474 SLG, backed by a .347 xwOBA that grades well above neutral, tells you the raw power is translating at the MLB level even though the 39.8% hard-hit rate looks ordinary. The gap between that xSLG and a middling xBA of .248 is the whole profile in miniature, he barrels enough balls to carry real power without being a consistent contact maker, and at 21.9% K% he's not a liability either, just not a weapon. Stewart projects to 34 home runs with a .806 OPS across 694 PA, and 16 stolen bases add a wrinkle you don't always get from a corner bat this big. If the contact shape stays as barrel-dependent as the Statcast profile suggests, he profiles as a solid everyday corner with above-average power rather than a star, but that's a real outcome.

Alonso's 94.0 mph average exit velocity and 55.4% hard-hit rate sit at the 98th percentile, and his .518 xSLG says the power translates to real damage when he connects — but a 27.2% whiff rate drags his actual average well below what that .273 xBA suggests is possible, and the projection lands at .247/.340/.461 across a full 698 PA. Thirty-three projected home runs from a first baseman with that kind of raw contact authority is a fine outcome, not a great one, and it holds only if his 11.3% walk rate keeps the on-base floor from caving every time the strikeouts spike. He's a middle-of-the-order thumper who leaves counting-stat value on the field every season he doesn't tighten the zone.

reports.name: Luis García Jr.
reports.published_report: The contact quality is elite; the plate discipline is the problem. García's xBA sits at .289 (95th percentile) and his xSLG at .507 (92nd), which is the production engine, but he's chasing 39.7% of pitches out of the zone and walking at just 4.6%, both near the bottom of the league. The swing-and-miss rate is actually fine at 15.6%, so when pitchers attack the zone he does damage, and that bat-to-ball skill translates to 30 home runs and an .852 OPS in 522 plate appearances if he keeps seeing hittable pitches. The whole profile hinges on whether pitchers keep feeding him strikes — the day they commit to working him away and forcing him to expand, that .279 average and those power numbers soften fast.

reports.name: Hunter Goodman
reports.published_report: Forty-three projected home runs from a catcher is the kind of number that stops a conversation, and Goodman's 16.3% barrel rate makes it believable — that sits at the 96th percentile and is the engine under everything here. The problem is sitting right next to it: a 33.9% strikeout rate at the 2nd percentile, paired with a 40.3% chase rate, means the power comes at a steep and persistent plate-discipline cost. At 37.9%, Lile is expanding the zone at a rate that suppresses his walk rate to 5.8% and keeps real contact damage limited — his 88.3 mph average exit velocity sits in the bottom third of the league, and the .312 xwOBA reflects a hitter who barrels the ball well enough (8.4%) but doesn't hit it hard often enough to carry a thin approach. What saves the profile is 29.3 ft/s sprint speed, genuine above-average wheels that turn marginal contact into hits, project 15 steals, and make the .248/.300/.421 projection line look more functional than the underlying contact quality suggests. If the chase rate comes down and he starts seeing more pitches, there's a second-division everyday outfielder here. If it doesn't, he's a useful bench piece whose legs do more work than his bat.

reports.name: Wilyer Abreu
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .487, well clear of what his .459 projected SLG implies, and a 13.1% barrel rate backs the shape of that gap. Abreu makes hard contact at a genuine clip, and the approach is quietly solid: 10.0% walks, 20.7% strikeouts, a chase rate that holds below the league middle. The whole profile hangs on whether the barrel production translates at scale across a full 672 projected plate appearances, because the average exit velocity at 90.1 mph is functional rather than elite, meaning he needs to keep finding barrels rather than overwhelming pitchers with raw force. If the barrels stay, you're looking at a legitimate 28-homer outfielder with a real .330 OBP; if contact quality regresses toward the average velo, the power dials back and you've got a serviceable regular who doesn't do any one thing loudly enough to carry a lineup spot.

reports.name: Nolan McLean
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is doing real work here: 28.5 K% puts McLean in the 86th percentile, and 207 punchouts across 178.3 projected innings is the kind of volume that holds a rotation slot together even when the peripherals are mixed. The chase rate, at 28.0%, is the uncomfortable number — hitters aren't biting out of the zone, which means the strikeouts are coming from whiffs and called strikes in the zone rather than manufactured expansion, and that's a narrower margin for error. His xERA sits at 3.63 and the projection slots him at a 3.50 ERA over 18 quality starts, a profile that holds if the command (8.8 BB%) tightens just enough to keep him from falling behind and losing the zone advantage he's already not getting for free. If the walk rate stays sticky and the chase rate doesn't improve, he slides toward a back-end arm who survives on strikeouts but works too deep into counts to sustain the innings load.

reports.name: Otto Lopez
reports.published_report: The .285 xBA grades in the 92nd percentile, and that's the whole engine here. Lopez makes contact at a 13.2% strikeout rate that almost nobody in the majors can match, and his 19.5% whiff rate says the contact is genuine: he's actually squaring balls up, rather than nicking them. The problem is a 4.9% walk rate that barely registers, which means the .344 OBP projection leans almost entirely on him continuing to find the barrel, and if pitchers start exploiting that 32.9% chase rate the on-base numbers get thin fast. With 30 projected stolen bases and a fielding grade in the 96th percentile at middle infield, the floor is a useful everyday regular even in a down-contact year, and the ceiling, if the bat plays true, is a .307 hitter who does a little of everything without truly punishing anyone.

The .282/.359/.459 line at AA is built on a real discipline foundation, 47 walks against only 60 strikeouts, and 32 stolen bases give the profile a dimension that survives even if the .177 ISO doesn't fully carry over, since the translation pegs the equivalent at .139, a tick below average. A 31.7% whiff rate and a .209 xBA put him in the bottom rungs of the league at actually hitting the ball, and the .288 xwOBA confirms the damage — that's a below-average offensive profile even before accounting for sequencing. What saves the projection is the 91.0 mph average exit velocity and the legs: 39 projected steals give him a floor as a counting-stat contributor even when the bat goes quiet. If the strikeout rate doesn't bend, the .219/.298/.404 projection line is probably honest, and you're looking at a second-division regular who earns his roster spot with speed and positional flexibility rather than any offensive upside.

reports.name: Michael Busch

reports.name: Logan Gilbert
reports.published_report: The contact quality numbers are the one honest wrinkle in an otherwise clean profile. Gilbert's barrel rate sits at 10.4% and his hard-hit rate at 42.2%, both well below average, yet his 3.71 xERA and .299 xwOBA land in almost exactly the same place, which tells you the damage-suppression isn't doing the work you'd expect. What's actually keeping him at that level is command: a 5.8% walk rate that grades elite, paired with a 29.9% whiff rate and a 32.9% chase rate that keep hitters uncomfortable enough to give up easy counts. The projection, 3.46 ERA and 201 strikeouts across 190.7 innings, holds up as long as the contact quality doesn't consolidate, because if hitters start squaring him up at a higher rate, the walk rate alone won't bail him out.

reports.name: Mason Miller
reports.published_report: A 48.4% strikeout rate. Hitters are averaging 85.1 mph off the bat against him, barrels arrive at just 3.8%, and the 37.6% chase rate explains why: they swing at his stuff out of the zone because they have no choice, and they still miss nearly half the time they do connect. reports.name: Grant Taylor
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.44 and the xwOBA at .244, both in the 98th percentile, and the fastball is running 98.2 mph — that combination explains why contact, when it does happen, goes nowhere dangerous. His 32.6% strikeout rate does the heavy lifting, driven by a 34.1% chase rate that forces hitters to expand, and the 28.4% whiff rate says he's finishing them when they do. The walk rate at 7.9% is the one lever: if command slips and that number climbs, the whole structure gets leaky, because he's not suppressing hard contact through weak contact so much as through avoiding it entirely. If the control holds, the projection's 2.46 ERA across 81.7 innings with 12 saves looks like a fair read on a genuine late-inning weapon in Chicago.

reports.name: Sam Antonacci
reports.published_report: The contact profile here is genuinely unusual: a 14.7% whiff rate and a 22.9% chase rate that together push his xBA to .284, yet his average exit velocity sits at 87.6 mph with a 36.1% hard-hit rate that ranks near the bottom quarter of the league. He makes elite contact on balls he reaches, but he doesn't reach many with authority. The projection fills that out to a .271/.359/.400 line across 564 PA, which profiles as a useful everyday outfielder on a better roster than Chicago's, carried almost entirely by the bat-to-ball skills and 21 stolen bases rather than any power foundation. If the exit velocity doesn't grow with age, the .400 SLG ceiling is the ceiling, and this becomes a high-average, low-slug regular whose value lives and dies with the batting average holding close to his .284 xBA.

reports.name: Juneiker Caceres
reports.published_report: The discipline line at 18 years old in A+ is what makes you look twice. Juneiker Caceres has walked and struck out exactly 36 times apiece across A+ & A this season, a 12/12 BB%/K% split that translates to a K-rate below league average and a BB-rate just above it at the MLB equivalent level. The .311/.409/.516 across 291 plate appearances is loud on its face, and a .324 BABIP keeps it honest enough that the shape isn't doing all the heavy lifting. reports.name: Dustin May
reports.published_report: The fastball grades out beautifully, 96.9 mph and 2326 rpm, and then the contact suppression profile refuses to follow. A 45.7% hard-hit rate and 90.1 mph average exit velocity against him are genuinely ugly numbers, which is the central tension in everything Dustin May does: he can blow it by hitters at the point of offering, but the ones who make contact hit it hard. The strikeout and walk rates sit right at league average, the xERA lands at 4.04, and the projection calls for a 4.26 ERA over 161.3 innings, so what you're looking at is a mid-rotation profile built on a premium fastball that hasn't found a way to make the contact profile match. reports.name: Zach Ehrhard
reports.published_report: The .407 OBP is doing the heavy lifting here, and the translation shows why it travels. Zach Ehrhard's 16% walk rate at AAA in 2026 converts to 12.6% at the MLB level, nearly half again what most big-league hitters draw, while his strikeout rate lands right at league-normal, making the on-base approach look genuine rather than level-dependent. The power is the question mark: a .185 ISO at AAA shrinks to .149 in translation, essentially league average, which means if the bat speed or launch angle doesn't play up, he's a center fielder who gets on base rather than one who punishes mistakes. Bench or platoon bat is the honest ceiling, but a bench bat who posts OBPs like that, steals 17 bases, and doesn't strike you out is a real roster piece.

reports.name: Jake Bennett
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is built almost entirely on location and discipline, not swing-and-miss. Bennett's 36.6% chase rate sits at the 95th percentile while his 23.4% whiff rate is below the median, a combination that says hitters are chasing pitches they aren't missing, which is a contact-management approach with a very specific vulnerability: if his command slips, the whole structure falls apart, because the stuff at 92.9 mph with 2152 rpm on the fastball isn't going to bail him out. What keeps the profile credible is the 5.2% walk rate and a 5.2% barrel rate that suggest he's executing the plan consistently enough — the .272 xwOBA and 3.04 xERA paint a genuinely good pitcher, and the projection's 3.57 ERA over 124.9 innings reflects some regression toward contact outcomes rather than dismissing the underlying control. The floor, if the command wavers or the chase rate normalizes, is a soft-tossing back-end starter living on borrowed time; the ceiling, if he keeps the zone discipline intact, is a mid-rotation piece who earns his outs the hard way.

reports.name: Nate Snead
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument here. Across AA & A+, Snead has issued just 22 walks in 89 innings, a 2.2 BB/9 that ranks in the 95th percentile of the pitcher pool, and the MLB-equivalent translation comes out at 2.8 while the league sits at 3.2. The strikeout side is the problem: 76 punchouts across AA & A+ gives him a 7.7 K/9, and the MLB translation comes out at 6.9 where the league averages 8.6, which is why the K-BB% lands at 15% in the minor-league pool but shrinks to 11.3% once the run environment shifts. If the command holds at the upper levels and the stuff generates enough weak contact to compensate for below-average swing-and-miss, there's a back-end piece here; if it doesn't, the profile is a depth arm with a polished walk rate and not much else to carry it.

reports.name: Patrick Copen
reports.published_report:
The strikeout rate translates. Everything else is the problem.

At AA in 2026, Patrick Copen has racked up 101 strikeouts across 82.3 innings, and that 11.0 K/9 moves to an 8.9 MLB-equivalent, roughly league average for a starter. The walk rate doesn't make the same trip: 60 walks in those same innings produces a 6.6 BB/9 at AA, and the translation puts that at 5.8 at the MLB level, nearly double what pitchers in that role typically allow. That gap between the strikeout ceiling and the control floor is the whole profile, a 1.7 WHIP and a 6.80 ERA at a level where the ball isn't supposed to be flying around like that. If the command ever rounds into shape, there's a depth arm here; if it doesn't, the strikeouts just make the walks more expensive.

reports.name: Ben Kudrna
reports.published_report:
Two innings. That's the entire current AAA sample, and it's doing almost no work here.

What the translation shows isn't alarming but isn't encouraging: a K/9 that matches the MLB average exactly at 8.6, a BB/9 of 3.8 where the average sits at 3.2, and a K-BB% of 12.4 when the typical MLB starter lands at 13.5. If the strikeout rate doesn't climb and the walks stay where they are, the profile resolves as a depth arm, which is exactly where the ceiling lands anyway. The honest read here is that 2.0 IP can't tell you much, and ValuCast's rankings reflect that uncertainty, sliding him six spots in three days.
